```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.25)
```

This development interface estimates landscape scales and response effects
together in a Bayesian model. It accepts stacked observations, such as the same
sites surveyed over several years. Annual scales can borrow information from a
common distribution, an approach called partial pooling.

Start with `vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")` for kernel preparation
and `vignette("year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR")` for annual maps.
See `vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")` to distinguish
posterior targets, likelihood calculations and prediction uncertainty.
The worked example below shows actual NUTS fits, annual scale estimates and
predictive checks. Compact posterior draws are bundled with the package so
you can read the fitted results without installing sampling software. The
long fitting calls are shown but are not rerun during a package build. Full
sampling is the primary workflow; approximation methods follow later.

## Check your setup

Preparation and the stored example need no optional Bayesian packages. Before
fitting your own model, check the packages required by your chosen method:

```{r setup-check}
check_bayes_setup(method = "prepare")
```

For full sampling, install RTMB, tmbstan, rstan and posterior, then run the
dependency check in your R session:

```{r install-sampler, eval=FALSE}
install.packages(c("RTMB", "tmbstan", "rstan", "posterior"))
check_bayes_setup(method = "sample")
```

`ready = TRUE` means the required packages load and meet their minimum
versions. It does not test compilation, available memory or a model's
sampling behavior. Source installation can require a C++ compiler. On Windows,
follow the [Rtools instructions](https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/)
for your R release. The [RStan setup guide](https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started)
and [RTMB installation page](https://github.com/kaskr/RTMB) explain their
platform requirements. This interface uses tmbstan and RStan; installing
CmdStan alone does not supply those R packages.

You can validate your observations, maps and formulas with `method = "prepare"`
before installing the sampler. Run a small fit next and inspect its
diagnostics. More iterations can improve simulation precision, but they
cannot repair an inappropriate likelihood or an uninformative landscape.

## Response year effects and scale year effects

These formulas describe different parts of the model:

```{r formulas}
response <- count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site)
scales <- list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year))
```

In the response formula, `factor(year)` lets baseline expected counts differ
among years. The site random intercept accounts for repeated observations at
the same site. The habitat coefficient describes its association with the
response after surrounding habitat has been weighted by distance.

The scale formula gives each year its own log landscape scale. Those annual
values share an estimated mean and between-year standard deviation. A year with
little scale information can borrow information from the other years. This is
the hierarchy $\log D_y = \alpha + \tau z_y$, with $z_y \sim N(0,1)$.
Here $D_y$ is the year's kernel scale in map units, $\alpha$ is the population
log-distance location and $\tau$ describes variation among annual log scales.
The priors on $\alpha$ and $\tau$ are specified separately from response effects.
The annual effects are exchangeable: this hierarchy does not impose temporal
autocorrelation.

Use `~1` for one shared scale, `~year` for fixed factor-year scale effects, or
`~1 + (1 | year)` for partial pooling. Treat calendar year as a factor when
you want separate annual effects. A numeric year specifies a linear trend in
log scale; center it to give the intercept a useful meaning.

For a comparison without estimated pooling, use `~0 + year`. Each factor level
then has its own log-scale coefficient with a normal prior centered at the same
log median distance and SD `scale_intercept_sd`. This avoids making the first
year a privileged prior reference. The priors still regularize the separate
annual estimates; this is not an unpenalized likelihood fit.

## Model flexibility and current limits

Scale formulas describe log distance, so they can include measured covariates
as well as group effects. For example, a centered numeric year can describe a
trend while an annual random intercept allows departures from it:

```{r scale-formula-options}
trend_and_year <- list(habitat = ~1 + year_centered + (1 | year))
two_predictors <- list(
  habitat = ~1 + (1 | year),
  forest = ~1 + (1 | year)
)
crossed_groups <- list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year) + (1 | region))
```

The corresponding columns must exist in the data, and both kernel predictors
must be prepared for the two-predictor example. Separate predictors have
separate scale parameters and independent prior group effects. Using the same
group name does not introduce an estimated correlation between their scales.

Full NUTS can fit multiple scale-group SDs. The marginal approximation currently
integrates exactly one scale-group SD and rejects models with more than one.
Additional response random intercepts are distinct from this limit. Broad
simulation evidence is strongest for one landscape predictor with annual
pooling and Gaussian kernels; a valid formula is not itself evidence of good
identification or interval calibration for a more complex model.

The response can be Gaussian, Poisson, binomial or negative binomial, with the
documented links. Binomial data can use successes and failures. Gaussian and
exponential kernel means are supported. The response formula allows offsets,
ordinary fixed covariates and additive random intercepts. Preparation checks
the complete model before optional sampling software is needed.

The landscape coefficient currently stays common across years even when its
scale varies. Kernel-by-year interactions and response random slopes are not
supported. The interface also lacks correlated random effects, temporal
autoregression, spatial random fields, zero inflation, custom families and
joint detection or multispecies likelihoods. These would require explicit
likelihood, design and validation work. Bayesian inference alone does not add
them to the package. Existing likelihood wrappers support some models outside
this Bayesian interface, so it is not a replacement for every existing backend.

Use posterior summaries and predictive checks for the fitted observations.
For new observations and unobserved years, see
`vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")`. It shows separate
policies for new scale and response effects, future landscape scenarios and
joint predictive totals. A fixed response year factor cannot predict an
unseen year's coefficient; the forecasting example uses annual response
random effects instead.
Hierarchical scale models are new capabilities of this development interface;
they are not exclusive to Bayesian inference in statistical theory.

## Prepare annual maps and stacked observations

The artificial example has five annual habitat maps and repeated surveys at
25 possible sites. Two years have fewer surveys. Counts were generated with
NB2 overdispersion, a habitat response effect, annual baseline differences and
site random intercepts. The generating kernel scales vary among years.
Projected distances are meters in this example.

```{r prepare-data}
example <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "bayesian-annual-example.rds",
  package = "multiScaleR"))
dat <- example$data
inputs <- example$inputs
knitr::kable(example$truth, digits = 0,
  caption = "Generating kernel scales and surveyed observations by year.")
```

The stored inputs are numeric bin summaries, not live raster pointers or a
sampling object. To reproduce the maps and data, use the bundled source:

```{r regenerate-data, eval=FALSE}
source(system.file("examples", "bayesian-annual-data.R", package = "multiScaleR"))
fresh <- make_bayesian_annual_data()
dat <- fresh$data
inputs <- fresh$inputs
```

That script prepares the site-year observations with
`kernel_prep_by_group(points, maps, group = as.character(dat$year),
max_D = 1200, sigma = 250, nbins = 48, store_cell_data = FALSE)`.
It computes the generating response from the same finite-cell bins used for
inference. `sigma = 250` is the preparation reference, while the table above
contains the distinct generating annual scales. See the annual-map vignette
for a walk-through of preparing your own maps.

The key `site_year` identifies a prepared observation and its annual landscape.
The `site` column identifies repeated surveys at the same location. When one
static landscape is reused over time, a repeated site ID can instead map several
observation rows to the same prepared row. Do not reuse static bins when the
intended annual landscape changed.

```{r prepare-model}
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(
  response, inputs, dat, scales = scales, row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2", priors = list(scale_median = 250),
  method = "prepare"
)
prepared
```

Preparation fixes observation order, checks formulas and missing values, and
defines priors. It does not estimate parameters or produce posterior draws.
Kernel columns are rebuilt from the bins at each sampled scale.

### Check what the priors imply before fitting

Simulate complete datasets from the prepared prior model. This needs no
optional Bayesian software and does not condition on the observed counts.

```{r prior-predictive}
prior <- simulate_bayes_prior(prepared, nsim = 100, seed = 63)
prior_checks <- data.frame(
  statistic = c("Fraction of zeros", "Largest count"),
  observed = c(mean(dat$count == 0), max(dat$count)),
  prior_lower = c(quantile(vapply(prior$responses, function(y) mean(y == 0),
    numeric(1)), .025), quantile(vapply(prior$responses, max, numeric(1)), .025)),
  prior_upper = c(quantile(vapply(prior$responses, function(y) mean(y == 0),
    numeric(1)), .975), quantile(vapply(prior$responses, max, numeric(1)), .975))
)
knitr::kable(prior_checks, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The bounds describe variation among simulated dataset statistics, including
parameter and observation variation. They are not confidence intervals around
the observed statistic. Broad count ranges can arise from the joint priors on
response coefficients, site variation and dispersion. Decide whether those
ranges are scientifically plausible for your survey design before fitting;
the table does not select a prior or establish model fit. The simulation keeps
the prepared maps, offsets, trial totals and predictor standardization fixed.
`prior$means` excludes observation variation. `prior$log_scales` stores log
distance by group and replicate for inspecting scale quantiles separately.

In these 100 replicates, the central zero-fraction range is
`r format(round(prior_checks$prior_lower[1], 2), nsmall = 2)` to
`r format(round(prior_checks$prior_upper[1], 2), nsmall = 2)`, compared with
`r format(prior_checks$observed[1], nsmall = 2)` observed. The largest-count
range reaches about
`r format(round(prior_checks$prior_upper[2]), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)`,
compared with an observed maximum of `r prior_checks$observed[2]`.
These priors often generate count patterns quite different from the observed
data. Review their implications using biological knowledge and the survey
design. The stored fits retain their original priors so that the comparisons
continue to describe the same posterior.

## Sample and inspect the posterior

This call fits the annual hierarchy. The example uses more iterations than
the function's default to obtain stable displayed results. Chains run serially.

```{r sample, eval=FALSE}
fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  response, inputs, dat, scales = scales, row_id = "site_year",
  family = "nbinom2",
  priors = list(scale_median = 250, scale_group_sd = 0.5),
  chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 5211,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12)
)
fit
summary(fit)$diagnostics
```

Sampling includes response coefficients, annual scales, site effects,
between-group SDs, and NB2 dispersion. Laplace approximation is disabled.
Chains run serially.

Diagnostics report rank-normalized R-hat, bulk and tail effective sample sizes,
divergences, tree-depth hits, and energy behavior. The passed flag requires at
least two chains, R-hat no greater than 1.01, bulk and tail effective sample
sizes of at least 100 per chain, no divergences or maximum-depth hits, and
E-BFMI of at least 0.3. Inspect individual parameters when a flag fails.
Good mixing does not rule out missed modes or establish model adequacy.

Check the fitted annual distances as well as the raw coefficients. Annual
log distance combines the population location, group SD and annual deviation;
those combinations can mix differently from their individual components.

```{r derived-diagnostics, eval=FALSE}
precision <- diagnose_bayes_scales(fit)
precision$parameters  # Rhat and effective information for annual log distances and SDs
precision$quantiles   # endpoints and medians with Monte Carlo standard errors
precision$passed      # requires the original sampler checks AND the derived checks
```

The derived screen uses the same Rhat and effective-sample-size cutoffs.
`mcse` estimates simulation error in each quantile, in the stated units.
For annual log distances, an MCSE of 0.01 is on the log axis. It is not the
posterior uncertainty about that year's distance. Compare computational
precision with the decision you need to make: passing the screen does not
guarantee a stable lower endpoint. Inspect independent runs when tails matter.
The function leaves the original sampler flag unchanged.

The stored fits were run with the calls described here. Diagnostics were
computed before retaining 2000 joint posterior draws per fitted model. Keeping
complete parameter vectors preserves dependence among annual scales,
coefficients, site effects and SDs. The original samplers are not bundled.

Consequently, `diagnose_bayes_scales()` cannot compute new chain diagnostics
from these compact fits. It reports `available = FALSE` and explains why;
the original diagnostic evidence remains in the example. Approximate draws
also cannot supply MCMC chain diagnostics. Inspect their stored numerical
checks instead.

```{r stored-fit}
fit <- example$fits$pooled
knitr::kable(example$fit_info[c("model", "iterations", "original_draws", "stored_draws", "seconds")],
  digits = 1, col.names = c("Model", "Iterations/chain", "Full draws", "Stored draws", "Seconds"),
  caption = "Actual fitting effort and compact stored draws.")
knitr::kable(example$fit_info[c("model", "max_rhat", "min_bulk_ess", "min_tail_ess",
  "divergences", "depth_hits", "min_ebfmi", "passed")], digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Model", "Rhat", "Bulk ESS", "Tail ESS", "Div.", "Depth", "E-BFMI", "Pass"),
  caption = "Diagnostics from all unthinned chains and derived scale quantities.")
```

**How to read the diagnostics:** each model must pass the original sampler
checks and separate checks on derived scale quantities. `max_rhat` should be
at most 1.01, `min_bulk_ess` and `min_tail_ess` at least 400 for four chains,
and divergences and depth hits zero. `min_ebfmi` should be at least 0.3.
These checks use all retained chain iterations, rather than treating the
smaller bundled draw count as additional evidence. If a longer retry was
needed, its actual iteration count appears in the table and the original
failed attempt remains in the development study.

## Read annual estimates and population variation

```{r annual-results}
annual <- posterior_scales(fit)
knitr::kable(annual[c("group", "median", "lower", "upper",
  "p_below_min_D", "p_above_max_D")], digits = 3)
summary(fit)$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd
coefficients <- summary(fit)$coefficients
knitr::kable(coefficients[c("coefficient", "median", "lower", "upper")], digits = 3)
```

**How to read the output:** `median`, `lower` and `upper` describe each year's
kernel scale in meters. The interval is a central 95% credible interval,
conditional on the model, priors and prepared landscapes. The population SD
describes variation among years on the log-distance axis. It is distinct from
uncertainty in one year's distance. The two support columns report posterior
mass outside the input reference range; large distances still use only the
neighborhoods that were extracted. These are separate marginal intervals,
not a simultaneous 95% band for all annual scales.

Response coefficients use the log expected-count scale. Exponentiating a
coefficient gives an expected-count ratio, holding the other predictors and
effects fixed. The habitat coefficient is shared across years and refers to
one SD of the landscape predictor under the fixed reference transformation.
Annual baseline coefficients change expected counts; annual scale effects
change distance weighting. They describe different ecological relationships.

For this NB2 example, the main output locations are:

| Quantity | Where to read it | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Response coefficients | `summary(fit)$coefficients` | Log expected-count effects; exponentiate for count ratios |
| Annual distances | `posterior_scales(fit)` | Fitted kernel parameters in meters, with marginal credible intervals |
| Population scale coefficients | `summary(fit)$scale_coefficients$habitat` | Log-distance intercept and any log-distance contrasts |
| Between-year SD | `summary(fit)$group_sd$log_scale_group_sd` | Population variation among annual log distances |
| Between-site response SD | `summary(fit)$group_sd$response_group_sd` | Site variation on the log expected-count axis |
| NB2 size | `summary(fit)$dispersion` | Theta in `variance = mu + mu^2 / theta`; larger theta means less overdispersion |

A between-year SD of 0.5 corresponds to a multiplicative distance factor
`exp(0.5)`, about 1.65, per population SD. It is not an annual distance's
posterior standard error. In a Gaussian response model, response coefficients
and response SDs instead use response units; binomial coefficients use log odds.

```{r annual-plot}
truth_points <- data.frame(
  group = annual$group, covariate = annual$covariate,
  truth = example$truth$scale[match(as.character(dat$year[annual$row]), example$truth$year)]
)
plot(fit) + ggplot2::geom_point(data = truth_points,
  ggplot2::aes(x = group, y = truth), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 4,
  color = "firebrick", size = 3)
plot(fit, type = "group_sd")
```

**How to read these plots:** points and vertical intervals summarize the
posterior. Red crosses show known generating scales, which would be unknown
in an empirical study. The SD plot separates annual scale variation from site
response variation because their units differ. A plot can display a fit whose
diagnostics failed, but its subtitle flags that failure. Plotting does not
establish convergence or calibration. Its subtitle uses stored numerical
flags; it does not recompute the derived annual-scale diagnostics.

The continuous half-normal prior on a group SD assigns no point mass to
exactly zero. A positive lower credible limit therefore does not establish
year-to-year variation. Assess the probability of variation large enough to
matter ecologically, and compare the shared-scale control. The SD's posterior
spread still describes uncertainty about the amount of pooling.

## Compare shared, independent and partially pooled scales

Keep the response model and coefficient priors the same while changing only
the scale model. The shared model uses one distance for all years. Independent
annual cells have separate coefficients with equal distance priors. The
hierarchy learns a population location and SD while estimating annual effects.

```{r comparison-fits, eval=FALSE}
shared <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, row_id = "site_year",
  scales = list(habitat = ~1), priors = list(scale_median = 250),
  chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 5212,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12))
independent <- multiScale_bayes(response, inputs, dat, row_id = "site_year",
  scales = list(habitat = ~0 + year), priors = list(scale_median = 250),
  chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 5213,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12))
```

```{r pooling-comparison}
comparison <- example$comparison
ggplot2::ggplot(comparison, ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = median,
  ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = model, shape = model)) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(position = ggplot2::position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = example$truth,
    ggplot2::aes(x = year, y = scale), inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 4, size = 3) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Year", y = "Kernel scale (m)", color = "Scale model",
    shape = "Scale model") +
  ggplot2::theme_bw()
knitr::kable(example$recovery, digits = 3,
  caption = "Log-scale error in this one artificial dataset.")
```

Black crosses mark the generating annual scales. Partial pooling can stabilize
weakly informed years, but it can also shrink an
unusual year too far toward the others. Compare the intervals with the sample
sizes and generating scales. Here, hierarchical log-scale RMSE is about 0.484,
compared with 0.586 for independent years. The shared model does better than
either, with RMSE about 0.359, despite the distinct generating annual scales.
This dataset has too little scale information to reward all the added annual
flexibility. The hierarchy's intervals contain all five generating scales,
compared with four for independent years and five for the shared model.
These are five related interval checks, not an estimate of 95% calibration.

The example illustrates the consequences of the scale model. One dataset
cannot establish comparative recovery or interval coverage. Do not choose an
empirical prior by minimizing an error against generating values that are
available only in a simulation.

## Check predicted counts and prior sensitivity

`predict()` describes expected responses at the fitted observations.
`simulate()` also includes observation sampling variation. Here are three
simple checks on the count distribution:

```{r fitted-means}
expected_counts <- predict(fit)
rows <- match(example$truth$year, as.character(dat$year))
expected_preview <- cbind(
  data.frame(year = dat$year[rows], observed = dat$count[rows]),
  expected_counts[rows, c("median", "lower", "upper")]
)
knitr::kable(expected_preview, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
  caption = "Expected counts for one fitted observation per year.")
```

**How to read the predictions:** `median`, `lower` and `upper` describe each
observation's expected count, including its fitted site effect. An observed
count need not lie in this interval because observation variation is absent.
The intervals are marginal for individual observations, not a simultaneous
band. `predict(fit, re.form = NA)` sets response site effects to zero while
retaining fitted annual scales; it does not average over a new site's effect.
For grouped-binomial models, expected-response predictions are success
probabilities, while simulations return success counts out of the trial totals.

For example, the displayed 2023 observation is zero although its interval for
the expected count is positive. A zero can still arise from the NB2 observation
distribution; it does not need to lie in an interval for the mean.

```{r predictive-checks}
replicate_counts <- simulate(fit, nsim = 200, seed = 94)
statistics <- function(y) c(mean = mean(y), zero_fraction = mean(y == 0), maximum = max(y))
replicated <- vapply(replicate_counts, statistics, numeric(3))
predictive <- data.frame(statistic = names(statistics(dat$count)),
  observed = statistics(dat$count),
  replicated_median = apply(replicated, 1, median),
  replicated_lower = apply(replicated, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  replicated_upper = apply(replicated, 1, quantile, 0.975))
knitr::kable(predictive, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The observed mean of `r round(predictive$observed[1], 2)` and maximum of
`r predictive$observed[3]` lie within their displayed replicate ranges.
The observed zero fraction of `r predictive$observed[2]` is nearer the upper
end, so inspect where zeros occur by year and site.

These are posterior predictive intervals for data summaries, not credible
intervals for a scale. A discrepancy can indicate that the response model
misses a feature of the counts. Agreement on three summaries is not a complete
model check. Also examine patterns by year, site and fitted mean for your data.

With five years, the prior on between-year variation can matter. The stored
example repeats the hierarchical fit using half-normal prior scales 0.25,
0.5 and 0.75 for the between-year log-scale SD. The median distance reference
remains 250 m, so predictor standardization is held fixed.

```{r prior-sensitivity}
knitr::kable(example$sensitivity, digits = 3,
  caption = "Population SD summaries under three explicitly specified priors.")
```

To reproduce the two alternatives, repeat the pooled fitting call with
`priors = list(scale_median = 250, scale_group_sd = 0.25), seed = 5214`
and with `scale_group_sd = 0.75, seed = 5215`. These are deliberate sensitivity
models, not changes to the function's defaults. Assess whether scientifically
important annual conclusions depend on a defensible prior choice. Stable
sampling alone does not establish that the data identify the pooling SD.
Here its posterior median rises from about 0.150 to 0.235 to 0.276 as the
half-normal prior scale rises from 0.25 to 0.5 to 0.75. The broad upper
interval limits also increase. With only five weakly informed years, the data
leave considerable uncertainty about the amount of annual variation.

## Choose a computation method

Full NUTS sampling is the main workflow in this guide. Alternatives change
the computation, not the likelihood or priors:

| Method | What it computes | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| `method = "sample"` | Joint posterior sampling by NUTS | Requires full-chain checks and adequate simulation precision |
| `method = "laplace"` | One local Gaussian approximation | Can miss skewness and dependence on a weakly identified SD |
| `method = "marginal"` | Numerical integration of one scale-group SD with conditional Gaussian approximations | Grid convergence does not establish accurate annual intervals |
| Marginal with `correction = "importance"` | Full-target weighting of proposed parameter vectors | Poor proposal coverage can make estimates unstable despite a large candidate count |

For formulas, controls, actual comparison outputs and interpretation of each
numerical flag, read `vignette("bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR")`.
The marginal approximation integrates exactly one scale-group SD in total.
Use full sampling for models with more scale-group SDs. A returned fit or a
passed numerical flag does not by itself establish adequate calibration.

## Distinguish distance uncertainty from population variation

### Prefer quantiles when distance tails are broad

Medians and credible intervals remain useful under broad distance uncertainty.
Arithmetic means and SDs need more care. The annual log-scale model includes
the product of a normal year effect and an uncertain between-year SD. With a
half-normal SD prior of scale `s`, the prior moment `E(exp(r * tau * z))` is
finite only when $r s < 1$. The default `s = 0.5` is already at the boundary
for the second distance moment. The prior-sensitivity choice `s = 1` is at the
boundary for the arithmetic distance mean.

The binned likelihood can retain these tails: as distance grows, kernel weights
approach uniform weights within the extracted neighborhood. A finite trace can
therefore return a sample mean or SD even when the corresponding posterior
moment is not finite. More draws cannot turn an infinite moment into a stable
estimate. This does not invalidate posterior medians or interval quantiles.

```{r log-scale-summary, eval=FALSE}
posterior_scales(fit)                 # distance medians and credible intervals
posterior_scales(fit, scale = "log")  # means and SDs on the log-distance axis
```

The log-distance SD measures uncertainty in one fitted year's distance. It is
different from the population SD describing variation among years. Exponentiate
log-distance medians or interval limits to return to map units. Exponentiating
a log mean gives a geometric summary, rather than an arithmetic distance mean.
The comparison studies use log-distance errors and distance quantiles, so their
primary recovery and calibration statistics do not require a finite distance
variance. These clarifications leave the fitted priors unchanged.

### Separate posterior uncertainty from Monte Carlo uncertainty

A credible interval describes posterior uncertainty about a scale. Monte Carlo
uncertainty describes how accurately a finite computation estimates that
interval or median. A flat posterior CDF near a quantile can turn a small
probability error into a substantial distance change. Inspect the quantile
MCSE from `diagnose_bayes_scales()` for an original NUTS fit and compare it
with the precision your scientific decision needs.

The original sampler flag checks raw parameters and sampler behavior. It does
not certify annual-median precision. Compare independent runs when tails
matter. Weighted importance summaries and their separate precision limits
are explained in `vignette("bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR")`.

## Prior and landscape support checks

Scale intercepts have normal priors on log distance, centered at the specified
median scale. Between-year log-scale SDs have half-normal priors. With few
years, the prior on between-year variation can substantially affect results.
Repeat the fit with defensible alternative median scales and group-SD priors,
then compare annual summaries and predictions.

Centering and SD for each kernel predictor are calculated once across fitting
observations at the prior median scale. They are held fixed during sampling,
giving response coefficient priors a fixed reference meaning. This differs from
scale-dependent standardization in existing optimization backends. Changing
the reference median changes that transformation too; inspect it when comparing
prior specifications.

`p_below_min_D` and `p_above_max_D` report posterior mass outside the input
reference range. Scales have no hard bounds. Each kernel still uses only cells
extracted within `max_D`; a large sampled scale cannot recover missing distant
habitat. Missing raster cells are excluded and finite weights renormalized.

Weak landscape effects may provide little information about scale. Partial
pooling and priors can stabilize estimation, but narrow intervals can reflect
the prior. General scale-recovery, calibration, and runtime studies remain
development gates.

## Quick reference

```{r quick-reference, eval=FALSE}
# 1. Validate explicit observation-to-map alignment.
prepared <- multiScale_bayes(
  count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site), inputs, dat,
  scales = list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)),
  row_id = "site_year", priors = list(scale_median = 250), method = "prepare"
)
# 2. Sample shared and annual parameters jointly.
fit <- multiScale_bayes(
  count ~ habitat + factor(year) + (1 | site), inputs, dat,
  scales = list(habitat = ~1 + (1 | year)),
  row_id = "site_year", priors = list(scale_median = 250),
  chains = 4, iter = 6000, warmup = 3000, seed = 521,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95, max_treedepth = 12)
)
# 3. Inspect diagnostics before interpreting scales.
summary(fit)$diagnostics
precision <- diagnose_bayes_scales(fit)  # full NUTS sampler required
precision$parameters
precision$quantiles                    # simulation error of annual log endpoints
posterior_scales(fit)
predict(fit)                        # uncertainty in expected counts
simulate(fit, nsim = 100, seed = 1)  # replicated observation counts
```

| Function | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `check_bayes_setup()` | Check optional package availability before fitting |
| `kernel_prep_by_group()` | Match stacked observations to annual maps |
| `multiScale_bayes()` | Prepare, sample, or approximate the hierarchical scale model |
| `simulate_bayes_prior()` | Check prior implications before fitting, using the prepared design |
| `posterior_scales()` | Summarize shared and annual scales in map units |
| `predict_scales()` | Predict scales at new covariates and years, including new-group variation |
| `diagnose_bayes_scales()` | Check annual log-scale mixing and quantile simulation error |
| `plot()` | Display fitted scale intervals or between-group SDs |
| `predict()` | Propagate posterior uncertainty into fitted or new-observation means |
| `simulate()` | Generate posterior predictive responses |

See also `vignette("bayesian-computation", package = "multiScaleR")` for
approximation choices and numerical precision,
`vignette("bayesian-prediction", package = "multiScaleR")` for new sites and years,
`vignette("year-specific-rasters", package = "multiScaleR")` and
`vignette("quickstart", package = "multiScaleR")`.
